sections.h2: Myrtle Beach housing at a glance
sections.html:
Myrtle Beach sits in Horry County on the Grand Strand. Population was 35,682 at the 2020 census, and 40,937 is the estimate for 2025. Older cottages stand near the oceanfront, while condos and subdivisions fill the inland side. The median home was built in 1992.

Whoever owns a house in town might live in it, retire in it or rent it to vacationers, and each of those uses is taxed differently. Owners who live on seasonal work or rental income also feel the January 15 bill, which arrives in a slow part of the year.

sections.h2: Coastal condition and what buyers check
sections.html:
Hurricanes are the biggest threat to a house on this coast. Buyers send inspectors to look at salt damage, wind-driven rain and flooding first, which means the roof covering, windows, siding, HVAC and crawl-space moisture.

Storm repairs left undone can block a mortgage, so some owners turn to a cash sale instead. Pull your insurance papers and your flood status before you list. Lenders ask for both, and the answers shape what a buyer can borrow.

sections.h2: Who bills Myrtle Beach property tax and where to pay
sections.html:
Real property tax for Myrtle Beach addresses is collected by the Horry County Treasurer. One bill goes to the owner of record and carries city, county and school district charges. Four Treasurer offices serve the area:

  • Conway (main): 1301 Second Avenue, Conway, SC 29526
  • Myrtle Beach: 332 Hinson Dr, Myrtle Beach, SC 29579
  • South Strand: 9630 Scipio Lane, Surfside, SC 29588
  • Stephen's Crossroads: 107 Hwy 57 North, Little River, SC 29566

Offices open Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Dial (843) 915-5470 for the main line. Payment works in person, by mail, through the night deposit box, online, or over the phone at 843-428-2126, and a convenience fee applies to cards.

Exemption questions and real property address changes go to the Tax Assessor at (843) 915-5040. Homestead questions go to the Auditor at (843) 915-5051.

The full amount is due by January 15, in the year following the tax year. Anything postmarked after that date picks up a penalty in three stages set by S.C. Code 12-45-180, and a missing bill is no defense.

Payment datePenalty added
January 163 percent
February 27 percent more
March 175 percent more, then tax execution

An installment payment program is available through the county. Delinquent properties go to a public tax sale held every year by the Treasurer. Call the office for the sale date and for how installments work.

Assessment on a house that is not your legal residence is 6 percent of fair market value, where a primary home gets 4 percent. Renting the place out more than 72 days in a year also removes the 4 percent ratio.

The Myrtle Beach Area Chamber of Commerce keeps a tax calculator at mbtaxcalc.com, which the city has pointed homeowners to. It describes a Tourism Development Fee credit for primary homeowners inside the city limits. Owner-occupied homes are the only ones that qualify, so ask the county for the numbers on your own parcel.

This split changes what a sale means. A vacation-rental investor and a full-time resident face very different bills, and a buyer who will live in the home needs to apply for the 4 percent ratio before the first penalty date passes.

Owing tax does not stop a sale. At closing the title company sends the Horry County balance out of your proceeds, provided the price is high enough to cover it. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff first, since the penalty steps fall on January 16, February 2 and March 17.

A workable sequence looks like this:

  • Phone the Treasurer for the balance, with a payoff figure that holds through your closing date.
  • Find out whether your parcel has been advertised for the yearly tax sale.
  • Hand the payoff letter to the title company so the county is paid at the table.
  • Check with the Auditor or Assessor how your legal residence status is recorded, because the next owner's bill depends on it.

If a tax sale comes before you sell, S.C. Code 12-51-90 gives the owner twelve months to redeem. The interest rate is 3 percent of the bid for months one to three, 6 for months four to six, 9 for months seven to nine and 12 for months ten to twelve. Selling ahead of the sale avoids that clock.

Cash buyers can close around a tax balance with no lender appraisal and no repair list, a real help when storm wear or a deadline is the problem.

When the value looks wrong, file a written objection with the assessor. S.C. Code 12-60-2510 sets the window at 90 days from the day the assessment notice is mailed.

Build the file before you write. Useful pieces are nearby sale prices, contractor estimates, photos of damage and a copy of the notice itself. If you are unsure which form fits, the Tax Assessor at (843) 915-5040 can point you to it.

sections.h2: What to bring when you call or visit
sections.html:
A short list saves a second trip to any of the four offices. Bring photo ID, your parcel or address, your latest tax bill if you have one, and any closing or contract date you are working toward.

Ask each office one clear question. The Treasurer answers what is owed and by when. The Assessor answers how the house is classified and how to object. The Auditor answers homestead questions. Write down the name of the person you spoke to and the date, then pass the figures to your title company.

Owners who inherited a house or who live out of town can usually handle most of this by phone or online. Payment through the Treasurer is available online, so a payoff can often be settled without a trip to Conway.

Work backward from the next penalty date. If January 15 is near, paying before it keeps the bill at its base amount, and a closing that slips past January 16 adds the first charge. After that the next steps come on February 2 and March 17, and on the last date the Treasurer can move to tax execution.

A house sale has its own pace: the contract, a title search, the payoff request and the closing. The tax balance only becomes a problem when a date on the tax calendar lands inside that window. Tell the title company the dates early so the payoff can be updated if the closing moves.

An owner facing the annual tax sale should treat that date as a hard stop. Once a parcel is sold, the twelve-month redemption period starts and the cost climbs every quarter. Closing before the sale is cheaper and simpler.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Myrtle Beach?
faqs.a: Horry County does, through its Treasurer. There is an office at 332 Hinson Drive in Myrtle Beach and a main office at 1301 Second Avenue in Conway.

faqs.q: When is Myrtle Beach property tax due?
faqs.a: January 15 is the deadline. Late payments pick up penalties on January 16, February 2 and March 17.

faqs.q: Can I pay my Myrtle Beach property tax online?
faqs.a: Yes, by check or by Visa, MasterCard or Discover through the county. Expect a convenience fee on cards.

faqs.q: Do rentals in Myrtle Beach get the 4 percent rate?
faqs.a: No, not once the home is rented more than 72 days in a year. It is then assessed at 6 percent like other real property.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Myrtle Beach house with back taxes owed?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company pays the balance from your proceeds at closing if the price covers it. Get a payoff figure from the Treasurer first.
